bibliography.abstract: This study examines how Austria’s dual education system generates unique commuting demands. Apprentices must regularly navigate educational travel to vocational schools as well as employment-like commuting to often spatial dispersed training companies, while facing youth-related restrictions in autonomous mobility and financial resources. However, the mobility implications of this institutional arrangement remain largely overlooked in both transport research and policy. To explore how apprentices perceive and manage these mobility demands, twelve semi-structured interviews were conducted with apprentices aged 16–23 in the Vienna metropolitan area and Upper Austria, consisting of urban, peri-urban and rural contexts. Interview data were analysed via qualitative content analysis. Findings reveal that apprentices face heightened transport poverty risks due to spatial inaccessibility, temporal demands, and limited resources, particularly in rural, peri-urban and town areas where insufficient public transport increases dependence on private motorised transport or social support networks. Spatial disparities in training locations and early work hours intensify negative consequences of time poverty, stress and exclusion risks. While some mitigate these challenges through household support or flexible modal choices, access to coping resources is uneven. Despite these objective constraints, many apprentices do not perceive themselves as disadvantaged due to the normalization of car dependency and long commutes; burdens intensify primarily when multiple constraints overlap. The study highlights apprentices as a group facing structural mobility vulnerabilities that remain underrepresented in policy discourse. It calls for spatially tailored mobility interventions and stronger coordination between transport, education, and youth policy sectors to ensure equitable access to vocational education.
bibliography.title: Between education and employment: How apprentices navigate commuting mobility challenges across spatial contexts in Austria

en.caveats: The findings are based on a small qualitative sample of twelve interviews, which limits statistical generalizability across the broader Austrian apprentice population.
en.what: This study analyzes the commuting challenges of apprentices in Austria's dual education system using qualitative content analysis of 12 semi-structured interviews with youth aged 16 to 23. The research covers urban, peri-urban, and rural settings across the Vienna metropolitan area and Upper Austria to examine how these students manage travel between vocational schools and dispersed training companies.
en.why: It identifies a distinct, structurally vulnerable group of young commuters who face heightened risks of transport and time poverty due to early working hours and poor public transit outside urban centers. The findings demonstrate that while car dependency and long commutes are highly normalized among these youth, actual coping resources like household support remain highly unequal.
